cards.q: Why are computers binary rather than decimal, given that a wire can carry any voltage?
cards.a: Because of noise. A wire's voltage sags and wobbles by hundredths of a volt, which is fatal if digits are a tenth of a volt apart — and nothing downstream can detect the error. With only two legal values separated by a wide no-man's-land, noise is discarded at every step instead of accumulating. You give up nine tenths of the wire's information capacity and gain that every value is exactly right or catastrophically wrong, never slightly wrong.

cards.q: Which real machine worked in decimal, and what does that prove?
cards.a: ENIAC (1945, University of Pennsylvania) stored each digit as a ring of ten circuits with one lit. It proves binary was a live engineering choice that won a fight, not an obvious truth discovered in hindsight.

cards.q: What is a transistor, in terms of what it does rather than what it is made of?
cards.a: A switch operated by electricity rather than by a finger: three connections — input, output, control. Voltage on the control lets current flow. Demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947 by Bardeen and Brattain, with Shockley's theory. A phone chip has over ten billion and nothing else.

cards.q: How do switches become arithmetic?
cards.a: Two transistors in series is an AND; in parallel an OR; one wired inverted is a NOT. Those three build everything. Addition is an XOR for the sum plus an AND for the carry (a half adder), chained so each carry feeds the next. Shannon's 1937 MIT thesis showed switching circuits and Boolean algebra are the same subject.

cards.q: What is a register, and why are there only a few dozen?
cards.a: A row of flip-flops holding one number, sitting physically adjacent to the arithmetic circuits — a signal travels a fraction of a millimetre, so it is the fastest storage in the machine. You cannot have millions because there is no room and the wires would be long enough for delay to dominate.

cards.q: Why is main memory built from a different technology than registers?
cards.a: DRAM uses one transistor and one tiny capacitor per bit, so it is far denser — billions of cells. The capacitor leaks, which is why it must be refreshed thousands of times a second (the D is for dynamic). The trade is density for speed: roughly 80 nanoseconds versus effectively zero.

cards.q: What, physically, is a memory address?
cards.a: A number naming one of billions of storage cells. Memory is literally a very long row of numbered boxes each holding a byte, with exactly two operations: load box N into a register, store a register into box N. Every data structure you have ever used is made of those two.

cards.q: Why is a byte eight bits?
cards.a: A decision, not a law. IBM's System/360 (April 1964) standardised eight because it held one character in IBM's encoding and because eight is a power of two, making address arithmetic a bit-shift rather than a division. Earlier machines used six, seven and nine. Eight won because System/360 won.

cards.q: What is the single idea that turns a calculator into a computer?
cards.a: Putting instructions in the same memory as data, encoded as numbers — the stored-program design, written down in the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC in June 1945 under von Neumann's name, recording work with Eckert and Mauchly.

cards.q: Name four consequences of instructions being data.
cards.a: Programs can be loaded rather than rewired (seconds, not days); programs can be stored on media, so software exists apart from a machine; a program can write a program, which is what a compiler and V8's JIT are; and a program can overwrite itself or another, which is the root of the buffer-overflow class of vulnerability.

cards.q: What is an instruction set architecture, and why does it matter to a Docker user?
cards.a: A fixed agreement mapping bit patterns to operations, wired into the processor. x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V are mutually unintelligible agreements, which is why a compiled binary for one will not run on the other, why images carry an architecture tag, and why exec format error happens.

cards.q: State the entire operation of a processor in four steps.
cards.a: Fetch the bytes at the address in rip; decode what that pattern means; execute it; advance rip by the instruction's length. Repeat forever. There is no notion of a program, a user, a file or a scheduler in the hardware — all of those are software.

cards.q: What is a jump, mechanically?
cards.a: A write to the instruction pointer. An if is a comparison plus a conditional write to rip; a loop is a backward write; a call is a write plus a note of where to return. Control flow is arithmetic on one register.

cards.q: The fetch-decode-execute loop never asks anything and never pauses. Why does that matter for the rest of operating systems?
cards.a: Because everything after it is an answer to: given a device with total obedience and no ability to notice a better use of its time, how do you get it to do more than one thing, safely, for more than one person?

cards.q: What do pipelining, speculative execution and out-of-order execution change about the model?
cards.a: Nothing observable — they are optimisations the processor is contractually required to make invisible. They matter because speculative execution's cache side effects are what Spectre exploits, which is why performance.now() was coarsened and SharedArrayBuffer now needs cross-origin isolation headers.

cards.q: What exactly is a JavaScript stack trace, at the machine level?
cards.a: A chain of saved instruction pointer values walked through memory, with each address mapped back to a function name using a table the runtime kept. That is why a stripped native binary gives hexadecimal, why source maps exist, and why collecting frames costs real time.

cards.q: Why does a native Node addon compiled on an Apple laptop fail inside a linux/amd64 container?
cards.a: A .node file is compiled machine code for one ISA. Loading it on another gives invalid ELF header. This is the actual reason host node_modules must never be copied into an image and must be installed inside the build.

cards.q: What is endianness and where does it surface in JavaScript?
cards.a: Which end of a multi-byte number is stored at the lower address. x86 and ARM are little-endian; network protocols conventionally use big-endian, hence network byte order. It surfaces as buf.readUInt32BE versus readUInt32LE.

cards.q: What does the machine that runs your JavaScript actually execute?
cards.a: Machine code. V8 parses your source into a tree, interprets it with Ignition, and for hot functions hands it to TurboFan (and since 2021 Sparkplug), which writes machine code into memory and jumps to it — the 1945 stored-program property used at run time, thousands of times per process.

cards.q: What was the situation Node 0 left, in economic terms?
cards.a: The most expensive object in the building sat idle for most of every hour, waiting on humans walking across rooms, on card readers, and on the gap between one person's booked slot and the next. Every mechanism in operating systems is a response to some version of that observation.

cards.q: What is a resident monitor?
cards.a: A program that stays in memory while jobs come and go, reading the next job, loading it, jumping to it, and regaining control when it finishes. It is the first operating system, and it is a loop.

cards.q: What was the first operating system, and what were its two halves?
cards.a: GM-NAA I/O, 1956, by Robert Patrick (General Motors) and Owen Mock (North American Aviation) for the IBM 704. GM-NAA is the batch monitor loop; I/O is a set of shared input/output subroutines so every program did not rewrite card and tape handling itself.

cards.q: What two lasting concepts came out of the I/O half of GM-NAA I/O?
cards.a: The device driver — code that knows one piece of hardware's bit-level protocol, written once — and the system library, shared code the system provides. The reason you write fs.readFile instead of issuing NVMe commands is a straight line from 1956.

cards.q: Why did job control cards have to be separate from the program?
cards.a: The monitor must read them before the job runs, and it may not be able to parse the job's language at all. So resource limits, accounts, and step definitions live in a small separate language — IBM's JCL, from OS/360 in 1964.

cards.q: Map a JCL job to a GitHub Actions workflow.
cards.a: JOB is the job; account and CLASS= are billing and runs-on; TIME=(,30) is timeout-minutes; EXEC steps are steps; DD statements declaring inputs and outputs are artefacts and needs. It is a pipeline definition file with worse syntax and better error messages.

cards.q: What is spooling and what general principle does it establish?
cards.a: Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line: while job N computes, job N+1's input is read to disk and job N−1's output is printed, all concurrently. The principle: when a fast producer meets a slow consumer, put a queue between them and let each run at its own rate.

cards.q: What was offline operation and why was it done?
cards.a: Using a cheap slow machine (an IBM 1401) to copy card decks onto tape, then carrying the tape to the expensive machine, which could read it far faster. It kept the expensive processor off the card reader's clock.

cards.q: In what precise sense is a CI runner a resident monitor?
cards.a: It is a process that stays alive polling a queue, receives a job, prepares an environment, runs its steps, reports status, tears down, and returns to polling. Patrick and Mock's loop with HTTPS where the tape drive was.

cards.q: Name three BullMQ design features that are 1956 batch-monitor problems.
cards.a: The stalled-job checker with a renewable lock is the crashed-worker problem; attempts and backoff are JCL's COND codes; the job timeout is TIME=. They are not analogous problems — they are the same problems.

cards.q: What did 1950s spooling not have to solve that your streams do?
cards.a: Backpressure with an unbounded producer. The tape was finite. An HTTP client reading a response slowly while your server writes fast is an unbounded queue in your heap — which is why write() returning false and the drain event exist and why ignoring them grows memory until the process is killed.

cards.q: Why does every real cron job need a lock?
cards.a: If a run takes longer than the interval, the next starts anyway and you have two. Kubernetes exposes this as concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. The problem is inherent to the batch model, not to cron.

cards.q: What three things were still broken after the resident monitor?
cards.a: The processor still stopped dead whenever a job touched a device (polling); control returned to the monitor only if the job chose to return; and the monitor was ordinary bytes any job could overwrite.

cards.q: Give the ratio that motivates interrupts, in modern terms.
cards.a: A processor executes ~10 billion instructions per second. Main memory is ~80 ns away (hundreds of instructions), an SSD read ~100 µs (a million), a cross-continent round trip ~100 ms (a billion). The gap between the processor and everything else is the central physical fact of computing.

cards.q: Describe the interrupt mechanism in the fetch-decode-execute loop.
cards.a: After completing the current instruction — never halfway, since a half-executed instruction is unrecoverable — and before fetching the next, the processor checks the interrupt line. If raised: save rip and flags, look up the handler address by interrupt number, set rip to it. A return-from-interrupt instruction restores everything.

cards.q: What is asynchrony, physically?
cards.a: A wire, and a rule about checking it between instructions. Code ran in the middle of other code without anything calling it, and the interrupted program has no mechanism by which it could detect that. Every async thing you have written bottoms out here.

cards.q: What is the IDT and how is it used?
cards.a: The Interrupt Descriptor Table: 256 entries on x86, each holding a handler address, with the idtr register pointing at it. The processor uses the interrupt number as an array index. It is a table lookup, nothing more.

cards.q: Name the three kinds of entry into the kernel that share the IDT.
cards.a: Hardware interrupts (a device raised a line — asynchronous), exceptions (the current instruction could not complete: divide by zero, invalid opcode, page fault — synchronous), and software interrupts (a deliberate trap, i.e. a system call). Every transition into the kernel is one of these three.

cards.q: What is an IRQ and why were conflicts a thing in the 1990s?
cards.a: An interrupt request line number, from the Intel 8259 PIC's eight inputs (fifteen when chained). There were only fifteen, so devices had to share or conflict. Modern machines use APIC and PCIe MSI-X, where the signal is a write to a special memory address, allowing dozens of vectors per device.

cards.q: Why must interrupts be maskable, and what is a critical section?
cards.a: Because an interrupt can arrive while a data structure is midway through a multi-step update, and a handler that walks it sees an inconsistent state. cli/sti bracket the region — a critical section. The same problem reappears as every race condition and every database isolation level.

cards.q: What are top halves and bottom halves, and where do you see the cost?
cards.a: The top half is the actual handler: acknowledge the device, note there is work, return. The bottom half — softirqs, tasklets, work queues — does the real processing later with interrupts enabled. You see it as the si column in top; high si on one core is unbalanced interrupt handling.

cards.q: What is receive livelock, and what fixes it?
cards.a: At over a million packets per second the machine does nothing but enter and leave interrupt handlers. The fix inverts the node: the driver disables interrupts and polls, because at high rates polling always finds work. Linux's mechanism is NAPI, switching modes automatically.

cards.q: State the general rule about interrupts versus polling.
cards.a: Interrupts win when events are rare; polling wins when events are dense. The same trade decides WebSocket push versus HTTP polling, database triggers versus batch scans, and filesystem watching versus periodic scanning.

cards.q: What is DMA and what does it imply about a network interrupt?
cards.a: Direct Memory Access: the device writes to main memory itself while the processor does something else. So an interrupt from a network card means the packet is already in memory, not that one is available for fetching. It is also why zero-copy techniques target the remaining software copies.

cards.q: Trace a packet from the wire to a JavaScript callback.
cards.a: NIC reassembles the frame → DMA into a ring buffer → MSI-X interrupt → driver top half schedules a NET_RX softirq → softirq walks Ethernet/IP/TCP and appends to a socket buffer → the socket's wait-queue callback adds its descriptor to an epoll ready list → your process's epoll_wait returns → libuv invokes the C callback → read() → HTTP parser → V8 → your handler.

cards.q: Your callback ran. Why did it run?
cards.a: Because a wire went high. The event loop is not the origin of asynchrony in your system; it is software that organises asynchrony the hardware creates.

cards.q: What is interrupt coalescing and when does it show up in your measurements?
cards.a: Network cards deliberately delay interrupts by tens of microseconds to batch packets (ethtool -c). It contributes to the gap when a client-observed latency exceeds server-side timing plus network transit — together with Nagle's algorithm and delayed ACK, whose interaction produces the classic 40 ms stall that setNoDelay(true) addresses.

cards.q: How is a webhook endpoint that queues a job and returns 202 the same pattern as a network driver?
cards.a: It is a top half: get out of the handler fast because the caller times out, and do the real work where you are allowed to take your time. Same pressure, same design, different scale.

cards.q: Why can protection not be implemented in software?
cards.a: Whatever check you write runs as instructions the offending program could jump past, overwrite, or never call. A guard the guarded party can remove is not a guard. Enforcement must be in hardware, below the level any instruction can reach.

cards.q: What is the mode bit?
cards.a: One bit inside the processor — not in memory — holding whether execution is in kernel mode (ring 0) or user mode (ring 3). Certain instructions are declared privileged and raise an exception if decoded in user mode.

cards.q: Name five privileged instructions on x86-64 and say what each protects.
cards.a: cli/sti (interrupts, so a program cannot freeze the machine), lidt (the interrupt table, so it cannot redirect handlers), mov cr3 (the page table root, so it cannot remap memory), in/out (hardware ports, so it cannot drive the disk), hlt (stopping the processor).

cards.q: Why does the mode bit alone not give isolation?
cards.a: An ordinary mov is not privileged, so a user program could still write over kernel memory. Hardware must also check which addresses a program may touch, on every access, from tables only the kernel can modify — first base-and-limit registers, later page tables.

cards.q: What is a segmentation fault, physically?
cards.a: A memory access the hardware refused, raising an exception, whose kernel handler delivers SIGSEGV, whose default action terminates the process. The word segmentation is a fossil from an older memory scheme; the mechanism today is paging.

cards.q: State the correct model of what the kernel is.
cards.a: Not a process — a mode the processor is in. Your process executes kernel code, on its own time slice, with the privilege bit raised, and returns. There is no separate kernel process being scheduled.

cards.q: Given that model, what do us and sy in top mean?
cards.a: us is time your process spent executing with the mode bit at user; sy is time your process spent executing kernel code on its own behalf. Both are charged to it — which is why process.cpuUsage() returns user and system separately.

cards.q: Why does a kernel bug panic the machine while a user-space bug kills one process?
cards.a: Because the failing code is the system; there is no process to terminate. That asymmetry is the entire argument for microkernels.

cards.q: What was Multics and why does its failure matter?
cards.a: A 1965 MIT/Bell Labs/GE project for a computing utility shared by mutually untrusting users, with eight hardware-checked protection rings. It was enormous and late; Bell Labs withdrew in 1969, and Thompson and Ritchie then wrote Unix in reaction. Every system you deploy to descends from that withdrawal.

cards.q: x86 has four rings. Why does everyone use two?
cards.a: The paging hardware only distinguishes supervisor from user anyway, and portable kernels cannot rely on an x86-only feature. Rings 1 and 2 sat unused for thirty years until early paravirtualised Xen; hardware virtualisation later added an effective ring −1 for hypervisors.

cards.q: Why is there no JavaScript that opens a file?
cards.a: Opening a file requires talking to a storage controller, which requires privileged instructions, which user-mode code cannot execute. Every capability your runtime appears to have is a request across this boundary, and the complete list of what it can ask for is the syscall table.

cards.q: Why can process.on('uncaughtException') not save you from a crash in a native addon?
cards.a: A bad pointer raises a hardware exception, delivered as SIGSEGV, and the process dies below the level at which V8 has any say. There is no JavaScript stack to unwind because the failure was not in JavaScript.

cards.q: Why does Chrome run one process per site, and what did it cost?
cards.a: Because Spectre showed that software separation inside one process (V8 isolates and contexts) is no defence against a hardware side channel. Site Isolation, fully shipped in Chrome 67 (May 2018), moves the boundary to the hardware one, at roughly 10–13% more memory. It is also why SharedArrayBuffer requires COOP and COEP headers.

cards.q: How is WebAssembly's security model a re-derivation of this node?
cards.a: A Wasm module has one linear memory, every access bounds-checked, no way to form a pointer outside it, and no instruction that reaches the host — only imported functions the host chose to provide, which is a syscall table built in software. WASI makes the resemblance total.

cards.q: What does --privileged actually grant?
cards.a: It stops dropping the capabilities that let a process reconfigure the kernel: loading modules, raw device access, changing interrupt configuration. It is close to giving the container the host. The right fix for a container needing one ability is a single --cap-add.

cards.q: eBPF runs user-supplied code in kernel mode. How is that reconciled with this node's rule?
cards.a: With a verifier: the kernel statically proves the bytecode terminates, that every memory access is in bounds, and that it calls only permitted helpers, before JIT-compiling it. A proof obligation substituting for a hardware boundary.

cards.q: What is the asymmetry that makes the syscall design work?
cards.a: The user program controls when the crossing happens; it does not control where it lands. One instruction switches the mode bit and jumps to one address the kernel registered in advance.

cards.q: Give the Linux x86-64 syscall ABI.
cards.a: Number in rax; arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9; the syscall instruction; result in rax, where a value between −1 and −4095 is a negated errno.

cards.q: Write console.log("hi") as machine-level operations.
cards.a: mov rax,1 (write); mov rdi,1 (stdout); mov rsi,message; mov rdx,2; syscall. Every layer above — V8, Node bindings, libuv, glibc — exists to arrange those five lines.

cards.q: Why must the kernel switch to a separate stack on entry?
cards.a: Trusting the user's stack pointer would let a program point it at kernel memory. Each process has a small kernel stack (typically 16 KB) used only while executing kernel code on its behalf.

cards.q: Why does the kernel never dereference a user pointer directly?
cards.a: A program can pass any address, including a kernel address, so a direct dereference would let any process read kernel memory via read(). All user memory goes through copy_from_user/copy_to_user, which validate ranges and handle faults — the most security-critical code in the kernel.

cards.q: What does a syscall cost, and what made it worse?
cards.a: Roughly 50–100 ns. KPTI, the Meltdown mitigation from January 2018, unmaps kernel memory from the user page table so every crossing also reloads the page table root and disturbs address translation — five to thirty percent on syscall-heavy workloads.

cards.q: What is Linux's stable ABI, and how does Windows differ?
cards.a: On Linux the syscall interface is permanent — Torvalds's rule that userspace is never broken. On Windows syscall numbers change between builds and the stable contract is one level up in ntdll.dll/kernel32.dll. This is why a static Go binary works in a FROM scratch container.

cards.q: Distinguish a library function from a system call, with an example of each and one that is both.
cards.a: strlen runs entirely in user mode. write must enter the kernel. printf is a library function that formats into a user buffer and calls write when the buffer fills or a newline appears.

cards.q: Why do logs sometimes stop just before a crash?
cards.a: Buffering. Output to a pipe or file is fully buffered (typically 4 KB) rather than line-buffered as to a terminal, so the last chunk is lost when the process dies abruptly. Every language has a version of this.

cards.q: State the principle that explains buffered I/O, epoll, sendfile, writev and io_uring at once.
cards.a: A system call costs far more than an instruction, so software batches work in user space to make fewer of them.

cards.q: Map five Node APIs to the syscalls they make.
cards.a: fs.readFile → openat/read/close on a threadpool thread; net/http → socket/bind/listen/accept4/read/write driven by epoll; setTimeout → no syscall, just the timeout argument to epoll_wait; spawn → clone/execve/pipe2/waitpid; crypto.pbkdf2 → no syscall at all, pure computation on the threadpool.

cards.q: Why is process.stdout synchronous to a terminal and asynchronous to a pipe?
cards.a: A terminal or file will not block for long, so Node does the write inline. A pipe can block indefinitely on a slow reader, so it is made non-blocking and buffered. Consequences: heavy logging in a terminal costs a syscall per call, and output can be lost on an abrupt exit under Docker where stdout is a pipe.

cards.q: What is seccomp and how does Docker use it?
cards.a: A filter — a small kernel-checked program — inspecting each syscall's number and arguments to allow, deny or kill. Docker's default profile blocks about 44 of ~350 calls including mount and module loading, which is why some tooling gets an unexplained EPERM. Kubernetes exposes it as seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault.

cards.q: How does gVisor work, and why is it slower?
cards.a: It implements the Linux syscall interface in a user-mode process (Sentry) and services a container's calls there, so an escape must break Sentry first. It works because this interface is the complete boundary. It is slower because each syscall becomes several real crossings.

cards.q: Give a concrete case where syscall count is the performance problem.
cards.a: fs.appendFileSync per log line makes openat, write and close each time — three crossings per line. Holding the descriptor and batching makes one per batch. At scale this is the difference between logging costing one percent of your loop and twenty.

cards.q: What does strace -c -f tell you that a profiler will not?
cards.a: How many of each system call the process made and how much time went into each. An idle Node server is one blocked epoll_wait; a loaded one is epoll_wait, a burst of read/write/futex, and back. It is the runtime made visible.

cards.q: Distinguish a program from a process.
cards.a: A program is a passive file on disk. A process is that program in execution plus every piece of state the execution needs and every resource it holds. One program can have many processes; the file is a recipe, the process is the cooking.

cards.q: List what the kernel keeps for a process.
cards.a: Identity (pid, ppid, group, session); saved registers; a memory map and page tables; the open file descriptor table; credentials; signal state; filesystem context (cwd, root, umask); scheduling state; resource limits and accounting; and namespace and cgroup pointers. In Linux this is struct task_struct, about 10 KB.

cards.q: Why must cd be a shell builtin rather than a program?
cards.a: The current working directory is per-process kernel state. A child process cannot change its parent's, so a separate cd program would change its own directory and exit.

cards.q: What do the process states R, S, D, T and Z mean?
cards.a: R running or runnable; S interruptible sleep (waiting, wakeable by a signal — where most processes are); D uninterruptible sleep (inside the kernel at a point where waking would corrupt state); T stopped by a signal; Z zombie — finished but its exit status not yet collected.

cards.q: Why can you not kill a process in D state, even with kill -9?
cards.a: It is inside the kernel holding state that signal delivery would corrupt, typically partway through a disk or network filesystem operation. It leaves D when the operation completes; if it never completes — a hung NFS mount, a detached block device — it never leaves. Fix the device or reboot.

cards.q: Why can a machine with idle processors show a load average of 40?
cards.a: Linux load average counts running and uninterruptibly-sleeping tasks. A stuck storage device puts many tasks in D state. Load average is not a CPU metric on Linux.

cards.q: What is a zombie, why can you not kill one, and how do you clear them?
cards.a: A finished process whose task_struct remains because its parent has not called wait(). It is already dead — you cannot kill it. You fix or kill the parent, at which point PID 1 inherits and reaps them. A loop that never reaps eventually exhausts the PID space.

cards.q: What happens to children when their parent dies?
cards.a: They are reparented to PID 1 (or the nearest subreaper) and keep running. This is how a process survives the terminal that started it.

cards.q: Why did Unix split process creation into fork and execve?
cards.a: The gap between them is a place where the child can adjust itself with ordinary calls — redirect output, drop privileges, change directory, close descriptors, join namespaces — before the new program starts. Shell redirection, pipes and container setup all live in that gap.

cards.q: Because a Node server is one process, name four things every request handler shares.
cards.a: One file descriptor table (so all connections share the limit), one address space (so a leak anywhere affects everything), one set of credentials, and one cgroup budget. Plus: a native crash takes all in-flight requests. That blast radius, not raw throughput, is the honest reason to run several processes.

cards.q: Why do cluster workers share no cache, no counter and no session state?
cards.a: Because separate processes have separate address spaces by definition. That single fact forces Redis into more architectures than any other consideration.

cards.q: How does cluster let several processes accept on one port?
cards.a: The primary creates the listening socket and passes the descriptor to the children over a Unix socket — possible because a descriptor is a per-process number pointing at a kernel object. Since Node 0.12 the primary round-robins connections, because kernel-level distribution was badly unbalanced.

cards.q: Contrast cluster with worker_threads in one sentence each.
cards.a: Cluster gives isolation: separate processes, separate heaps, separate everything, a crash contained. Workers give sharing: one process, one descriptor table, one PID, separate V8 isolates but transferable buffers and SharedArrayBuffer — and a V8 crash kills everything.

cards.q: Why is your container's entrypoint special?
cards.a: It is PID 1 in its PID namespace, so the kernel does not deliver signals with default actions to it, and it is expected to reap orphans. A plain node index.js with no SIGTERM handler ignores docker stop and is SIGKILLed ten seconds later.

cards.q: Why do --init and tini exist?
cards.a: Because Node does not reap orphans, and PID 1 is expected to. A container that shells out to subprocesses accumulates zombies without a proper init as PID 1.

cards.q: Define a Kubernetes pod in terms of a process's state.
cards.a: A set of containers sharing some parts of that state — the network namespace (hence localhost, hence they cannot both bind port 3000) and optionally the PID namespace — but not the filesystem unless a volume is mounted into both.

cards.q: Name five files under /proc/<pid>/ and what each answers.
cards.a: status (state, threads, RSS, context switches), fd/ (every open descriptor as a symlink — the leak diagnosis), maps (the address space), limits (effective resource limits), cmdline (arguments). Reading those five tells you more in thirty seconds than most instrumentation.

cards.q: Why is a process unable to detect that it was context-switched?
cards.a: Its entire execution state is its registers, and they were restored exactly. It has no mechanism by which it could notice — only by reading a clock and seeing time passed.

cards.q: List the steps of a context switch.
cards.a: Enter the kernel (always — via syscall, interrupt or timer); save the user registers; save the kernel-side state into the outgoing task; choose the next task; load its page table root into cr3; switch kernel stacks and restore its registers; return to user mode.

cards.q: What is the direct cost of a context switch, and what is the indirect cost?
cards.a: Direct: roughly 1–3 µs of instructions. Indirect and larger: the incoming process finds cold L1/L2 caches, a disturbed TLB, and branch predictors describing the wrong program — so it runs at a fraction of full speed until they refill. Several to tens of microseconds all-in.

cards.q: Why is a thread switch cheaper than a process switch — precisely which step is skipped?
cards.a: The cr3 load. Threads share an address space, so the page table does not change, the TLB is not disturbed, and the caches likely still hold shared data. That is the entire difference.

cards.q: What do voluntary and nonvoluntary context switch counts tell you?
cards.a: Voluntary means the process gave up the processor because it had nothing to do — normal and high for an I/O-bound service. Nonvoluntary means the kernel took it away because a slice expired or something more urgent appeared — a rising count means it wants more CPU than it is getting, from competition or a cgroup quota. Both in /proc/<pid>/status.

cards.q: Give the arithmetic argument for the event loop.
cards.a: Thread-per-connection pays a context switch per event: microseconds, with cold caches, plus ~100 KB of memory per connection. One thread handling many connections replaces the switch with a function call: nanoseconds, warm caches, no page table change. Three orders of magnitude, and that is the whole thesis.

cards.q: What does the event loop's advantage explicitly not claim?
cards.a: Anything about being faster at computation. It wins on concurrency of waiting and loses on parallelism of computing.

cards.q: Why is max_connections in Postgres typically 100–200 rather than 10,000?
cards.a: Postgres uses one OS process per connection, so each costs a task_struct, several megabytes of private memory, and a scheduler entry. A few hundred is a heavy load on the machine. Hence connection pools, and hence pgbouncer multiplexing thousands of clients onto dozens of real connections.

cards.q: Why does raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE above your core count not add capacity for crypto work?
cards.a: More runnable threads than cores means the kernel rotates them, paying the full switch cost while doing no extra work. The correct bound is cores for CPU-bound work; it may exceed cores for genuinely blocking work. Tell them apart by whether the threads sit in R or in D.

cards.q: What does the cs column in vmstat 1 indicate when it is very high?
cards.a: Hundreds of thousands of switches per second on a machine that is not obviously busy means thrashing: too many threads, lock contention, or a poll loop with a tiny timeout.

cards.q: What single piece of hardware makes preemption possible?
cards.a: A programmable interval timer raising an interrupt at a fixed rate. Control then enters the kernel regardless of what the program was doing, and the program cannot prevent it because cli is privileged.

cards.q: What is the historical difference between cooperative and preemptive multitasking?
cards.a: Cooperative (classic Mac OS through 9, Windows 3.x) meant a program kept the processor until it yielded, so one bad application froze the machine. Preemptive means the kernel can take it back. Everything mainstream has been preemptive for twenty-five years — except the JavaScript event loop.

cards.q: Name the five scheduling goals that conflict.
cards.a: Throughput (favours long slices), latency (favours short ones), fairness, priority (opposes fairness), and interactivity (a process that just got a keystroke should run now despite having no fairness claim).

cards.q: What did CTSS's multi-level feedback queue infer, and how?
cards.a: Which processes are interactive — from behaviour rather than declaration. A process using its whole slice is moved down (compute-bound, longer slice, less often); one that blocks early stays high. MIT, ~1961, Corbató.

cards.q: Explain CFS in one sentence, plus how it handles wake-ups.
cards.a: Every task carries a vruntime scaled by its weight, tasks live in a red-black tree ordered by it, and the scheduler always runs the smallest; a waking task is given a vruntime just below the tree's minimum so it runs almost immediately — interactivity falls out of the model rather than being a special case.

cards.q: What does one nice level change?
cards.a: Roughly ten percent of processor share — each step scales the task's weight by about 1.25. Range −20 to +19. nice -n 19 npm run build on a machine also serving traffic is a real and underused move.

cards.q: Name Linux's scheduling classes in priority order.
cards.a: SCHED_DEADLINE, then the real-time classes SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR (priorities 1–99, which preempt everything below and can hang a machine — hence sched_rt_runtime_us reserving 5%), then SCHED_OTHER (fair share, where everything you run lives), then SCHED_BATCH and SCHED_IDLE.

cards.q: Why are there per-core run queues, and what problem does that create?
cards.a: A single global queue would need a lock contended by every core on every decision. Per-core queues mean cores can idle while another is backed up, so a load balancer migrates tasks — reluctantly, because migration costs cache locality, and on a NUMA machine crossing sockets can halve memory performance.

cards.q: What is priority inversion, and what real incident is the standard example?
cards.a: A low-priority task holds a lock a high-priority task needs, and a medium-priority task preempts the low one — so the high-priority task is blocked by one it outranks. Mars Pathfinder, July 1997, resetting on the surface. The fix uploaded to the spacecraft was priority inheritance.

cards.q: Correct the claim that Node uses one core.
cards.a: Your JavaScript runs on one thread, so one Node process executes at most one of your functions at a time. The process also has libuv threadpool threads and V8 compiler and GC threads, which the kernel scheduler will run on other cores — so a Node process routinely exceeds 100% CPU.

cards.q: Explain the two-stacked-schedulers framing.
cards.a: The kernel scheduler is preemptive and arbitrates between processes and threads; the event loop is a scheduler too, deciding which callback runs next, but it is cooperative and regains control only when a callback returns. A 400 ms synchronous handler is a failure of the second, not the first — which is why the machine stays healthy while every other request in that process waits.

cards.q: In what sense is React's concurrent renderer this node reimplemented?
cards.a: It slices work into units, yields to the browser roughly every 5 ms via shouldYield(), assigns work to lanes by priority, and lets a keystroke interrupt a low-priority render. startTransition is nice; requestIdleCallback is SCHED_IDLE; scheduler.postTask is priority scheduling on the platform.

cards.q: Distinguish a Kubernetes CPU request from a CPU limit at the kernel level.
cards.a: A request becomes a cgroup weight — a relative share that only matters under contention. A limit becomes a quota: at most N ms of CPU per 100 ms period, enforced by stopping every thread in the container until the next period, even on an idle machine.

cards.q: What is the symptom of CPU throttling, and where is the evidence?
cards.a: Latency spikes at moderate average utilisation with no corresponding CPU graph. Evidence: nr_throttled and throttled_usec climbing in /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat, and rising nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches.

cards.q: Why does os.cpus().length lie inside a container?
cards.a: /proc/cpuinfo is not namespaced, so it reports the host's cores. Limits live in cgroup files, not in /proc. Use os.availableParallelism() (Node 18.14+).

cards.q: Why do two computers left alone disagree about the time?
cards.a: Every clock descends from a quartz crystal accurate to perhaps 20 parts per million — about 1.7 seconds of drift per day — and its rate changes with temperature. Disagreement is physical, not a software defect.

cards.q: Name the machine's clock sources and what each is for.
cards.a: The battery-backed RTC, read once at boot to initialise the system clock; the PIT and HPET, programmable timers that raise interrupts; and the TSC, a cycle counter readable in a couple of nanoseconds without entering the kernel, used for all high-resolution timing once processors gained an invariant, cross-core-synchronised version.

cards.q: What is a tickless kernel and why did it happen?
cards.a: Rather than a fixed HZ drumbeat, the kernel programs the timer for whenever the next thing is actually due. A fixed 1000 Hz tick meant a thousand interrupts a second even when idle — bad for battery, and catastrophic on a virtualisation host running two hundred idle guests.

cards.q: Distinguish CLOCK_REALTIME from CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
cards.a: CLOCK_REALTIME is wall-clock time since the 1970 epoch and can jump forwards or backwards when an administrator or NTP corrects it. CLOCK_MONOTONIC only increases and is meaningless as a date. Durations must use the monotonic one.

cards.q: Why is Date.now() - start a bug?
cards.a: It is a wall clock. An NTP correction mid-measurement can make the duration wrong or negative, which then flows into code assuming non-negative. Use performance.now() or process.hrtime.bigint().

cards.q: What is the difference between slewing and stepping a clock?
cards.a: Stepping jumps to the correct value, making time discontinuous. Slewing changes the clock's rate slightly until it catches up, keeping it monotonic. Standard practice is slew small corrections, step large ones; chrony converges much faster than the original ntpd, which matters on virtual machines.

cards.q: What happened on 30 June 2012 and what is leap smearing?
cards.a: A leap second triggered a Linux hrtimer livelock spiking CPU to 100% across huge numbers of machines and hanging Java applications; Reddit, Mozilla and Qantas's booking system went down. Leap smearing, now widespread, spreads the extra second over a 24-hour window as a tiny rate change so no discontinuity occurs.

cards.q: What is the vDSO and what does it explain about strace?
cards.a: A page of kernel-maintained code and data mapped read-only into every process, so clock_gettime reads the TSC and applies the parameters entirely in user mode, at ~20 ns and with no system call. It is why Date.now() shows no syscall in strace, and it appears as [vdso] in /proc/<pid>/maps.

cards.q: What exactly does setTimeout(fn, 1000) promise?
cards.a: A minimum, never a maximum. The timer fires only when the loop reaches its timers phase, so a running callback delays it, machine load delays it, and kernel granularity adds more. 1400 ms under load is not a bug.

cards.q: Why is setTimeout(fn, 0) not immediate?
cards.a: It is clamped — 1 ms in Node, and in browsers 4 ms once five nested timeouts have accumulated, a rule from 2010 because sites used it as a busy loop. For after-this-callback use a microtask; for after-I/O use setImmediate.

cards.q: What happens to timers in a background browser tab?
cards.a: Throttled to roughly once per second, and since Chrome 88 to once per minute after five minutes hidden. A setInterval poll stops and then bursts on return — which is why visibilitychange, SSE/WebSocket push, and refetchOnWindowFocus exist.

cards.q: Contrast the failure modes of setInterval and a self-rescheduling setTimeout.
cards.a: setInterval schedules from a fixed base, so async work taking longer than the interval produces overlapping executions — two requests in flight, or double processing. A setTimeout rescheduled at the end of the work cannot overlap but drifts by the work's duration each round. Choose knowing which failure you prefer.

cards.q: Why does a JWT library have a clockTolerance option?
cards.a: Because nbf and exp are wall-clock seconds and the issuing and verifying servers' clocks differ. A token issued by a server 30 seconds ahead is not yet valid to the verifier, failing with an error that reads like a code bug. TOTP and TLS certificate validation have the same problem.

cards.q: Distinguish Postgres now() from clock_timestamp(), and timestamp from timestamptz.
cards.a: now() returns the transaction start time and does not change within it; clock_timestamp() reads the actual clock each call. timestamptz stores an absolute instant in UTC; timestamp stores a wall-clock reading with no zone, which becomes unrecoverably ambiguous at a daylight-saving transition.

cards.q: Why can timestamps not order events across machines, and what is used instead?
cards.a: Clocks differ by milliseconds at best, so A's 10:00:00.100 and B's 10:00:00.050 tell you nothing about order. Systems use logical clocks (Lamport, vector), hybrid logical clocks, or Spanner's TrueTime, which returns a bounded interval and waits out the uncertainty. Practically: database sequences or ULID/Snowflake IDs, never client timestamps, and never last-write-wins by wall clock unless you accept discarding newer writes.

cards.q: What is the relocation problem?
cards.a: A compiler bakes absolute addresses into machine code, but the loader does not know where in physical memory the process will sit. Static relocation rewrites every address at load time (slow, and the copy cannot then be moved or shared); dynamic relocation adds a hardware base register to every address, so the program is compiled as if starting at zero.

cards.q: What is external fragmentation, with a concrete example?
cards.a: Free memory exists but not in one contiguous piece. Load processes of 100, 300, 200 and 400 MB in a 1 GB machine, exit the second and fourth: 700 MB is free in pieces of 300 and 400, and a 500 MB process cannot start.

cards.q: Why is compaction not the answer to fragmentation?
cards.a: It means copying gigabytes while every affected process is stopped. Allocation policies (first-fit, best-fit, worst-fit) reduce but never eliminate the problem.

cards.q: What were overlays and why do they matter to this chain?
cards.a: Programmers manually splitting a program into pieces and writing code to load one over another, ensuring no two mutually-calling pieces were swapped out together. It was a hated part of the job into the 1970s and is the reason virtual memory was pursued so hard.

cards.q: State the five requirements Node 9's failures impose on any memory design.
cards.a: Translate program addresses to physical ones in hardware; check permissions on every access; place memory non-contiguously so fragmentation cannot block; let a process exceed physical memory without programmer effort; and let two processes share the same physical memory.

cards.q: State the paging idea in one sentence, and say which of Node 9's failures it kills.
cards.a: Cut the address space into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, and let any page map to any frame. All five: fragmentation dies, protection is per-page, sharing is two tables pointing at one frame, and a page can be marked absent and fetched on demand.

cards.q: Why 4096 bytes?
cards.a: A balance: smaller pages waste less on the final partial page but need far more table entries; larger waste more and make transfers coarser. The VAX chose it in 1977 and it has survived a factor of a million in memory sizes, mostly because changing it would break too much.

cards.q: How is a virtual address translated, and why is it not a search?
cards.a: The address is cut in two. With 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset within the page, passed through untouched; the upper bits index the table. Translation is an array index and a concatenation — gate delays, not a search.

cards.q: Why is the x86-64 page table four levels of nine bits?
cards.a: Nine bits indexes 512 entries; 512 entries of 8 bytes is exactly 4096 bytes — one page. Every level of the tree is itself one page. 48 bits of address = 9+9+9+9 plus a 12-bit offset.

cards.q: What are the two facts that together constitute memory isolation?
cards.a: Changing cr3 changes the meaning of every address in the machine, and only the kernel can execute that instruction.

cards.q: Name the page table entry flags and what each enables.
cards.a: Present (is it in memory — if not the rest of the entry is free for the kernel's own bookkeeping); Writable (clearing it on a shared page gives copy-on-write); User/supervisor (how kernel memory is mapped everywhere yet unreachable); Accessed and Dirty (set by hardware, read by the kernel to choose evictions and writebacks); NX (non-executable, added by AMD in 2003, which is why shellcode on the stack no longer works and why a JIT needs special pages).

cards.q: Why does a four-level table not cost four extra memory accesses?
cards.a: The TLB caches recent translations — 64 to 1536 entries, fully associative — with hit rates well above 99% on ordinary code, because programs touch the same pages repeatedly.

cards.q: What problem do huge pages solve, and why do databases often disable transparent huge pages?
cards.a: A large randomly-accessed working set misses the TLB constantly; one 2 MB page covers 512 times as much memory per entry, so a 32 GB Postgres buffer pool needs vastly fewer. But transparent huge pages defragment in the background, causing latency spikes — which is why MongoDB and Redis tell you to turn THP off.

cards.q: List the six situations a single page fault can represent.
cards.a: Valid but not in memory (read it in — a major fault); valid and in memory but not mapped here (a minor fault); first touch of freshly allocated memory (find and zero a frame); a write to a copy-on-write page; growth just below the stack; or genuinely not part of this process — SIGSEGV.

cards.q: Why is it significant that all six are the same hardware event?
cards.a: Lazy allocation, demand loading, copy-on-write, growable stacks, memory-mapped files and segmentation faults are one mechanism distinguished only by kernel bookkeeping. It is the most elegant thing in the operating system.

cards.q: How do you distinguish major from minor faults, and what does a rising major count mean?
cards.a: ps -o min_flt,maj_flt or pidstat -r. Minor faults in the millions are normal and cheap. Major faults climbing in steady state means the machine is fetching pages from disk to run — thrashing — and it will show as latency no application profiler can explain.

cards.q: Define VSZ, RSS and PSS, and say which one matters.
cards.a: VSZ is total mapped address space — what the process asked for, including regions never touched. RSS is how many of those pages are actually resident — what it is using, and what a container limit and the OOM killer count. PSS divides shared pages among their sharers, so it is the honest number when summing across a process tree.

cards.q: Why is a Node process's VSZ often several gigabytes, and should you care?
cards.a: V8 reserves large regions of address space it may never populate, and address space is free on 64 bits. No — RSS is the number that consumes a resource.

cards.q: What is ASLR and what does it cost you when debugging?
cards.a: Randomising the addresses of stack, heap, libraries and the executable on every run so an attacker cannot predict where to jump. It is why native crash addresses differ every time and why symbolising a core dump requires knowing load addresses; randomize_va_space turns it off for debugging.

cards.q: Why does V8 use pointer compression, and what does it cap?
cards.a: Object references are stored as 32-bit offsets from a base: half the memory for pointers, and twice as many pointers per cache line so pointer-chasing misses half as often. It caps a single V8 heap at 4 GB of compressed address space — the real reason --max-old-space-size above ~4096 does nothing useful.

cards.q: What is a memory-mapped file and name three places it appears in your stack.
cards.a: Mapping a file's contents into the address space so reading it is reading memory, with pages faulting in on demand and shared through the page cache. SQLite and LMDB use it as their primary access method; V8 maps its startup snapshot (which is why Node starts in tens of milliseconds); and twenty containers from one image share the executable's text pages.

cards.q: Why is a Float64Array of a million numbers so much faster to loop over than a million {x,y} objects?
cards.a: Eight megabytes of contiguous, prefetchable memory versus a million pointers to a million scattered allocations, each access a potential cache miss at ~80 ns. Factors of five to twenty on numeric loops, and it is the memory hierarchy, not V8 being clever or stupid. It is also why columnar databases exist.

cards.q: Sketch a process's address space from high to low.
cards.a: Kernel space (mapped everywhere, supervisor-only); the stack, growing down; an unmapped gap; the mmap region (shared libraries, large allocations, mapped files, thread stacks); another gap; the heap, growing up; .bss, .data, .rodata, .text; and page zero, deliberately unmapped.

cards.q: Why does dereferencing null produce a fault rather than reading garbage?
cards.a: Page zero is deliberately left unmapped. The safety of null is a page-table decision.

cards.q: What is W^X, and what must a JIT do about it?
cards.a: No region is both writable and executable, enforced by the NX bit — which stops classical shellcode injection. V8 must break it: allocate pages, write machine code, flip them to executable, keeping the window narrow. Where it is forbidden entirely (iOS outside Safari, hardened kernels), JavaScript engines fall back to an interpreter and run several times slower.

cards.q: Why do the stack and the heap grow toward each other?
cards.a: A convention from when a process had one contiguous region: putting them at opposite ends let either grow into the shared middle. The unmapped gaps mean overgrowth faults instead of silently overwriting a neighbour.

cards.q: What is a stack frame and what is a stack trace?
cards.a: A frame holds one active call's locals, its extra arguments, and the return address; calling pushes, returning pops, and rsp points at the top. A stack trace is that chain walked.

cards.q: Why do you see RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded rather than a segmentation fault?
cards.a: V8 imposes its own smaller limit (~1 MB) and checks it on function entry so it can throw a catchable JavaScript error before the hardware guard page is reached. Hence ~10–12,000 frames rather than a hundred thousand, varying with locals per frame.

cards.q: Why is raising --stack-size past the OS stack a bad trade?
cards.a: It turns a catchable RangeError into a hard segmentation fault. Deep recursion in JavaScript is a design problem — engines still do not implement proper tail calls outside Safari — so the fix is an explicit stack, a queue, or iteration.

cards.q: What are the only two ways a program gets more memory?
cards.a: brk/sbrk, which moves a single heap-top pointer (so memory returns only from the top), and mmap, which requests a region of address space with stated properties and is what everything modern uses.

cards.q: Name the four kinds of mmap and one use of each.
cards.a: Anonymous private (plain memory — a large malloc, a JavaScript heap); file-backed private (an executable's data section, copy-on-write); file-backed shared (mmap I/O and shared memory between unrelated processes); anonymous shared (state shared between a process and its children, and /dev/shm).

cards.q: Why is MAP_ANONYMOUS memory guaranteed zero-filled?
cards.a: Security, not convenience: without it a fresh allocation could contain another process's freed data. The kernel keeps a supply of pre-zeroed pages.

cards.q: What will you see in /proc/<pid>/maps for a running Node process?
cards.a: The node binary's r-xp text and its data; an anonymous [heap]; many large anonymous regions that are V8's spaces and the allocator's arenas; mapped shared libraries including any .node addons; one stack per thread; and [vdso] and [vvar].

cards.q: Name V8's heap spaces and what each is for.
cards.a: New space (young generation, 1–8 MB per semi-space, allocation by pointer bump, collected by copying survivors to the other half — sub-millisecond); old space (promoted objects, mark-sweep-compact, mostly concurrent since Orinoco); large object space (over ~128 KB, never moved); code space (executable JIT output).

cards.q: What is the generational hypothesis and what does it imply for your code?
cards.a: Most objects die young, so collection cost scales with surviving data rather than allocated data. Ten thousand short-lived objects per request cost almost nothing; ten objects per request added to a module-level cache cost increasingly much, forever.

cards.q: Read the five numbers from process.memoryUsage().
cards.a: heapTotal and heapUsed are V8's spaces only; external is memory held by C++ objects tied to JavaScript ones, including buffers; arrayBuffers is the ArrayBuffer subset; rss is the operating system's number — all of the above plus the binary, libraries, thread stacks and allocator overhead.

cards.q: What is the signature of a buffer leak, and why is it hunted in the wrong place?
cards.a: Rising rss and external with a flat heapUsed. Most Node leak tooling looks at the heap, where these bytes do not appear, and --max-old-space-size cannot protect you because the limit only governs old space.

cards.q: Why must --max-old-space-size be meaningfully below the container limit?
cards.a: Because RSS exceeds old space by hundreds of megabytes of binary, libraries, code space, stacks, buffers and fragmentation, and the kernel kills on RSS.

cards.q: Is malloc a system call?
cards.a: No. It is ordinary unprivileged library code inside your process that obtains large regions with mmap or brk and carves them up — which is the fact that explains most of this node.

cards.q: Why does writing before the start of an allocated block corrupt the heap?
cards.a: The allocator stores a small header immediately before the returned pointer recording the block's size. Overwriting it breaks bookkeeping, and the crash appears much later somewhere unrelated.

cards.q: Describe glibc's allocator in three points.
cards.a: Free blocks kept in bins by size so finding a fit is not a linear scan; requests above MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KB, dynamically adjusted) get their own mmap and are returned to the kernel exactly when freed; and each thread gets its own arena — capped at eight times the core count — so threads do not contend on one lock.

cards.q: Why does free() usually not reduce RSS?
cards.a: It returns the block to the allocator's own free lists inside your process, so the next malloc can reuse it without a system call. Correct behaviour, and it means process memory is a high-water mark rather than a current measurement.

cards.q: Give two reasons memory cannot be returned even when the allocator wants to.
cards.a: The heap shrinks only from the top, so one small live allocation near the top pins everything below it; and a page can only be returned if every object on it is free, so a page holding one live 32-byte object stays fully resident.

cards.q: Account for the gap between heapUsed of 200 MB and a container using 800 MB.
cards.a: V8's heapTotal headroom; external memory (buffers, ArrayBuffers, addon allocations); the node binary and shared libraries (50–100 MB resident); V8's code space; thread stacks; and glibc arena fragmentation — often the largest surprise on many-core machines.

cards.q: What does MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 do and when is it worth setting?
cards.a: Caps the number of glibc arenas, trading a little allocation contention for substantially less resident memory. It is one of the few genuinely useful environment variables for containerised Node and Java services with unexplained RSS.

cards.q: Why do people LD_PRELOAD jemalloc?
cards.a: jemalloc and tcmalloc are designed around fragmentation avoidance and multi-threaded scalability, and swapping glibc's allocator without recompiling routinely reduces RSS by twenty to forty percent on allocation-heavy workloads. Sometimes 'our service uses too much memory' has a one-line answer involving no code.

cards.q: State the three layers of allocation.
cards.a: The kernel hands out pages via mmap; the allocator carves those into objects; the garbage collector decides which objects are reachable and returns the rest to layer two — which usually does not return them to layer one.

cards.q: Why is 'unreferenced' the wrong model for garbage collection?
cards.a: Collection traces reachability from roots — the global object, the call stack, handles held by native code. Anything unmarked is garbage. This is why tracing can collect a cycle and pure reference counting cannot.

cards.q: Name five ways a JavaScript memory leak actually happens.
cards.a: A module-level Map or array growing per request; an event listener added per connection and never removed, retaining its whole closure; a setInterval closing over a large object; a promise that never settles, retaining its continuation and captured scope; and V8's shared closure context, where an unrelated small closure keeps a large captured variable alive.

cards.q: How do GC pauses show up, and what actually fixes them?
cards.a: A scavenge is sub-millisecond; a full mark-compact of a 2 GB old space is tens to low hundreds of milliseconds, mostly concurrent but with a real compaction stop. It appears as p99 spikes uncorrelated with request complexity; find it with --trace-gc or a PerformanceObserver on gc entries. The fixes are architectural — allocate less per request, keep the live set small, split large heaps across processes.

cards.q: Derive a heap cap for a 1 GB container, and say what happens if you set none.
cards.a: Roughly 60–75% — 640 to 768 MB — then measure. With no cap, V8 derives its default heap size from the host's physical memory, so on a 64 GB node a 512 MB container gets a V8 that will not collect urgently until well past the point the kernel kills it.

cards.q: Why does work_mem in Postgres multiply dangerously?
cards.a: It is per sort or hash operation, per plan node, per concurrent query — so a modest-looking value can multiply by a hundred under load and exhaust the machine. It is the Postgres version of setting no heap cap.

cards.q: Why does a native addon leak produce a flat heap graph and no GC activity?
cards.a: It calls malloc directly, so V8 does not know that memory exists, does not count it towards the heap limit, and feels no pressure from it. napi_adjust_external_memory exists so well-behaved addons can tell V8; many do not.

cards.q: What is demand paging and what does it explain about cold starts?
cards.a: The kernel does not read a program into memory; it marks pages absent, records where they live, and jumps to the entry point, faulting pages in as they are touched. It is why a program starts in milliseconds regardless of size, and why the first request to a fresh process is slower — the code paths it exercises are being faulted in.

cards.q: What is the page cache, and why is low free memory healthy?
cards.a: All otherwise-unused memory is used to cache file pages; every ordinary read and write goes through it. Free memory is doing nothing, cached memory saves disk reads and is instantly reclaimable. Read available, not free.

cards.q: What happens on a write() to a file, before any fsync?
cards.a: Your bytes are copied into a cache page, the page is marked dirty, and the call returns. No disk has moved. Kernel threads write back later, governed by vm.dirty_ratio, dirty_background_ratio and dirty_expire_centisecs.

cards.q: How does the kernel approximate LRU cheaply, and what does the active/inactive split prevent?
cards.a: Hardware sets the accessed bit on any access; the kernel periodically clears and re-reads them — the clock or second-chance algorithm. Two lists mean a page must be referenced while inactive to be promoted, which stops one large sequential read from evicting the whole useful working set (cache pollution — why a nightly backup used to slow a database for an hour).

cards.q: What is a working set and what is thrashing?
cards.a: Denning, 1968: the set of pages a process has touched recently, a good predictor of what it will touch next. If the sum of all working sets exceeds physical memory, every fault evicts a page another process is about to need — the machine spends all its time moving pages and none doing work, and it collapses rather than degrading.

cards.q: Why do file-backed pages not need swap but anonymous pages do?
cards.a: A file-backed page's home is the file, so it can always be dropped. Heap, stack and anonymous mappings have nowhere to go without a dedicated swap area — without swap they can never be evicted at all.

cards.q: Why did Kubernetes historically refuse to run with swap enabled?
cards.a: Swap makes memory limits unenforceable and latency unpredictable — a page from RAM is 80 ns, from an SSD ~100 µs, a thousand times slower — and the scheduler's model assumes memory is memory. Support returned gradually from 1.28 onward, but for latency-sensitive services the default position is still no swap.

cards.q: Why does Linux overcommit memory?
cards.a: It has to in practice: fork plus copy-on-write doubles address space that will almost never be realised, and programs reserve large sparse regions they never touch — V8 among them. vm.overcommit_memory controls the policy.

cards.q: Why does the OOM killer use SIGKILL and what does that cost you?
cards.a: A page fault on legitimately-granted memory with no frame available has no sensible failure path — mov has no error return. So the kernel kills the highest scorer outright. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so there is no flush, no close, no draining, and no log line.

cards.q: Decode exit codes 137, 143 and 139.
cards.a: A process killed by a signal reports 128 + the signal number. 137 = 128+9 = SIGKILL (in a container, almost always the cgroup OOM killer). 143 = 128+15 = SIGTERM, a normal shutdown. 139 = 128+11 = SIGSEGV.

cards.q: Why can a container be OOMKilled on a machine with plenty of free memory?
cards.a: The cgroup memory limit is a separate, per-container OOM domain. It exhausted its own budget, not the machine's.

cards.q: How can a container with no memory leak at all be OOMKilled?
cards.a: Page cache from the container's own file writes is charged to its cgroup. Under memory pressure with heavy write throughput — logs, a temp file, SQLite, an upload buffer — it can be killed with anonymous usage far below the limit. Symptom: OOMKilled with a flat heap; evidence: the anon/file split in memory.stat.

cards.q: Why is choosing which limit you hit first a design decision?
cards.a: Hitting V8's heap limit throws a catchable fatal error with a stack trace and can trigger --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit — diagnosable. Hitting the kernel's limit produces one line in the host's kernel log and nothing else.

cards.q: Why does Postgres deliberately keep shared_buffers modest?
cards.a: It expects the operating system's page cache to hold the rest, accepting double buffering because the kernel's cache and readahead are good. effective_cache_size is not an allocation but a planner hint about total caching — set too low, it makes the planner avoid index scans it should choose. It is also why a tight container memory limit hurts Postgres in a way more shared_buffers does not fix.

cards.q: Explain a serverless cold start in terms of this node.
cards.a: The first invocation faults in the runtime, the dependency tree and JIT-compiled code page by page from storage. Hence bundle size affecting cold start more than steady-state performance, and hence snapshot-based fixes (Lambda SnapStart, V8 snapshots, --snapshot-blob) attacking it by having the pages already laid out.

cards.q: How does a process know whether it is the parent or the child after fork()?
cards.a: The call returns twice: the child's PID in the parent (or −1 on failure) and 0 in the child. That is the only asymmetry in the whole call.

cards.q: Describe copy-on-write step by step.
cards.a: The child gets its own page table pointing at the same physical frames; every writable page is marked read-only in both and flagged COW; reads are free and fully shared; a write raises a protection fault; the kernel allocates a fresh frame, copies 4 KB, points the writer's entry at it, marks both writable, and re-executes the instruction.

cards.q: What does forking a 2 GB process actually cost?
cards.a: The page tables and nothing else — a millisecond or two. If the child immediately execs, essentially zero pages are ever copied. This is why overcommit is a practical necessity, not just a permissive default.

cards.q: What is clone() and why is it the most clarifying call in Linux?
cards.a: One system call whose flags say exactly what the new task shares — address space, descriptors, signal handlers, namespaces. fork shares almost nothing; a thread shares almost everything; a container adds namespace flags. Threads, processes and containers are one system call with different arguments.

cards.q: Why can Redis memory nearly double during BGSAVE?
cards.a: It forks to get a frozen consistent view, which is nearly free — if the parent is not writing. Under heavy writes the parent dirties pages and each is copied. It is also why Redis explicitly recommends vm.overcommit_memory=1: with the default heuristic the fork itself can fail.

cards.q: Why can you not safely fork() a Node process?
cards.a: fork duplicates only the calling thread, but every lock the other threads held stays held forever by threads that no longer exist. If a libuv or V8 thread held the allocator lock, the child deadlocks on its first allocation. POSIX permits only async-signal-safe functions between fork and exec, and malloc is not one.

cards.q: What do cluster.fork() and child_process.fork() actually do?
cards.a: Spawn a brand-new node process via posix_spawn and execve, with an IPC channel attached. They are not the fork() system call — the name is inherited vocabulary, and confusing the two is a common interview stumble.

cards.q: Name five places copy-on-write appears above the kernel.
cards.a: Docker image layers (copy-up on first write, at file granularity); filesystem and cloud disk snapshots (block granularity); Postgres MVCC (a new row version rather than an overwrite — hence VACUUM); Git's immutable content-addressed objects (hence free branching); and React/Immutable structural sharing (new objects only along the path to the change — hence identity comparison as a change check).

cards.q: When you meet a system claiming cheap snapshots or cheap branching, what should you ask?
cards.a: What it costs when things do get written. That is almost always copy-on-write, and the write path is where the cost was deferred to.

cards.q: What is shared between threads of one process, and what is private?
cards.a: Shared: the address space and everything in it, the descriptor table, credentials, the current directory, signal dispositions, resource limits, cgroup and namespaces. Private: registers including the instruction pointer, the stack, the thread ID, the signal mask, errno, priority, and thread-local storage.

cards.q: Why can threads pass data in nanoseconds and also corrupt each other?
cards.a: Both come from the same fact — a shared address space with no boundary between them. You cannot take one property without the other.

cards.q: What flags turn clone() into a thread rather than a process?
cards.a: CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD — share the address space, filesystem context, descriptors, signal handlers and thread group. Linux schedules tasks; processes and threads are both tasks.

cards.q: What is fatal about the N:1 green-thread model?
cards.a: If one user thread makes a blocking system call, the kernel blocks the whole process and every other thread stops, because the kernel cannot know they exist. 1:1 (Linux NPTL, 2003) gives each user thread a real kernel task.

cards.q: Where do Go's goroutines and Java's virtual threads sit?
cards.a: M:N on top of 1:1 — a runtime scheduler multiplexing many lightweight threads onto a pool of kernel threads, crucially intercepting blocking operations so a blocked goroutine parks rather than blocking its thread. They are an event loop hidden inside the runtime, with a different ergonomic choice.

cards.q: List the threads in a busy Node process.
cards.a: The main thread running the event loop and all your JavaScript; four libuv threadpool threads by default; V8's background threads for concurrent marking, sweeping and compilation; and any threads created by native addons.

cards.q: How does knowing which thread is busy localise a Node performance problem?
cards.a: Busy main thread = a blocked event loop, and the fix is in your code. Four busy threadpool threads with an idle main thread = threadpool saturation, and the fix is sizing or offloading. Busy V8 background threads = GC pressure, and the fix is allocation behaviour.

cards.q: Why does a worker_thread get its own V8 isolate rather than sharing objects?
cards.a: JavaScript has no memory model for concurrently mutated objects, and a garbage collector that moves objects cannot safely do so while another thread holds raw pointers. The restriction is forced by the language, not chosen for simplicity.

cards.q: Distinguish postMessage, transferList and SharedArrayBuffer.
cards.a: postMessage deep-copies via structured clone — expensive for large payloads and unable to carry functions or prototypes. transferList moves an ArrayBuffer: ownership passes, the sender's becomes detached, constant time regardless of size. SharedArrayBuffer is genuinely shared pages — the one place JavaScript has real shared mutable memory, and the one place it can have a data race.

cards.q: Give the rule for choosing between the four concurrency options in Node.
cards.a: Workers for CPU-bound work when you want cores (a pool created at boot, never one per request — each costs a V8 isolate). The threadpool for blocking I/O. A separate process for isolation or a separate heap. The event loop for everything else.

cards.q: Why do Web Workers have no DOM?
cards.a: The DOM is a large mutable object graph with no locking and no memory model; permitting concurrent access would require synchronisation on every DOM operation. So the platform's position is that the DOM is single-threaded, permanently, and OffscreenCanvas and SharedArrayBuffer exist to make the boundary less painful.

cards.q: Postgres chose processes and MySQL chose threads. What does each buy?
cards.a: Postgres gets crash isolation and must arrange shared memory explicitly (shared_buffers is a shared mapping). MySQL gets cheaper connection creation and a naturally shared buffer pool, at the cost that one backend corrupting memory takes the server down. Neither is wrong, and the choice predicts connection-scaling behaviour.

cards.q: Why is counter++ not atomic?
cards.a: It compiles to three instructions — load, add, store — and two threads can interleave between any two of them. Both load 5, both compute 6, both store 6: two increments, one net effect. Nothing was written incorrectly.

cards.q: Define atomic, race condition, and data race.
cards.a: Atomic: an operation no other thread can observe partway through. Race condition: the result depends on the relative timing of operations that were not made atomic. Data race: two threads accessing the same location with at least one write and no synchronisation — in C/C++ formally undefined behaviour, so the compiler may assume it never happens.

cards.q: Why must concurrency correctness be established by reasoning rather than testing?
cards.a: Races are timing-dependent and do not reproduce. One in ten million iterations passes every test on a laptop and fails twice a week in production, sensitive to core count, load, compiler version, and whether a profiler is attached.

cards.q: What is cache coherence and what does it cost?
cards.a: Each core has its own L1/L2, so hardware must keep copies consistent — MESI, where a line is Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. To write, a core must broadcast an invalidation and wait for every other core to drop its copy: tens to hundreds of cycles over the interconnect.

cards.q: What is false sharing and why is it invisible in a profile?
cards.a: Two threads writing to two different variables in the same 64-byte cache line bounce that line between cores on every write, because coherence works at line granularity. The code is correct and throughput collapses by an order of magnitude. The fix is padding, which is why high-performance structures are littered with alignment attributes.

cards.q: Why can identical concurrent code be correct on x86 and broken on ARM?
cards.a: Memory ordering. x86's TSO model only lets a store appear after a subsequent load; ARM and POWER have weak models where almost anything can be reordered. This stopped being niche when Apple Silicon and Graviton became ordinary development and deployment targets.

cards.q: How does the compiler break concurrent code that looks correct?
cards.a: It hoists loop-invariant reads, keeps variables in registers instead of re-reading memory, and merges or eliminates stores — all valid under the assumption that no other thread is looking. A loop polling a flag can be optimised into an infinite loop.

cards.q: What is compare-and-swap and why is it called universal?
cards.a: Atomically: if this location holds the value I expect, replace it and tell me whether it did. lock cmpxchg on x86, load-linked/store-conditional on ARM. Every lock, lock-free queue, reference counter and atomic increment is built from it.

cards.q: Recognise optimistic concurrency at three scales.
cards.a: The CAS retry loop in hardware; a Postgres UPDATE ... WHERE version = $expected retried on zero rows affected; and an HTTP If-Match with an ETag. Same pattern, same failure mode — under high contention the retries dominate and you need a lock.

cards.q: What exactly does JavaScript's single thread protect you from?
cards.a: Data races only. Run-to-completion means nothing observes or modifies your objects while your synchronous code runs, so counter++ is safe. It does not protect you from race conditions.

cards.q: Why is a read-check-write across an await a race?
cards.a: Every await is a yield point: the function suspends, the loop runs other callbacks including another invocation of the same function, and it resumes against state that may have changed. Two concurrent transfers can both read balance 100, both pass the check, and both write 50.

cards.q: Give the three correct fixes for that transfer bug.
cards.a: Make it atomic in the database (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1, checking the row count); take a lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction, or an advisory lock); or use a version column with a retry. The same fixes a threaded program would use.

cards.q: What is a cache stampede and why is storing the promise the fix?
cards.a: if (!cache.has(k)) cache.set(k, await fetch(k)) issues N concurrent fetches for N concurrent requests, because every check happens before any set. Storing the promise means the second caller finds one in flight and awaits it. Recognising it as check-then-act is what tells you the fix.

cards.q: Why does Atomics exist in JavaScript, and why is Atomics.wait banned on the browser main thread?
cards.a: It exists because SharedArrayBuffer is genuinely shared memory and therefore the one place JavaScript can have a data race; the operations compile to the lock-prefixed instructions. Atomics.wait blocks, which would freeze the page.
