cards.q: In what sense is a database isolation level a memory model?
cards.a: Both are specifications of which interleavings a participant may observe. Read committed permits non-repeatable reads, the database equivalent of a compiler not being required to re-read a variable; Postgres SERIALIZABLE uses optimistic concurrency and can abort you with a serialization failure requiring the same retry loop as CAS.

cards.q: How is an idempotency key a compare-and-swap?
cards.a: A retry racing an original is the same interleaving problem; checking and inserting the key atomically is compare-and-swap over the network. Once you have seen the pattern at the instruction level the distributed version needs no separate learning.

cards.q: When is a spin lock right and when is it catastrophic?
cards.a: Right when hold time is shorter than a context switch — a few hundred nanoseconds — and there are more cores than contenders, which is true inside a kernel and almost never in application code. Catastrophic on a single core: the spinner cannot progress until the holder runs, and the holder cannot run until the spinner is preempted.

cards.q: Why is test and test-and-set better than plain test-and-set?
cards.a: Spinning on a write means each attempt acquires the cache line exclusively, saturating the interconnect and slowing the actual holder. Spinning on a plain read can be satisfied from a shared line, and only the final attempt writes.

cards.q: What is the futex's key property?
cards.a: The uncontended path never enters the kernel. Acquire is a compare-and-swap in user space — a few nanoseconds; only on failure does it call futex(FUTEX_WAIT, ...) to sleep on a kernel wait queue keyed by that address. Release wakes only if it can see a waiter.

cards.q: Why is a high futex count in strace -c meaningful?
cards.a: Because uncontended locks make no system calls at all, so futex calls are direct evidence of genuine contention.

cards.q: What is a semaphore and how does it relate to a mutex?
cards.a: Dijkstra, 1965: a counter with atomic decrement-and-wait-if-negative and increment-and-wake. Initialised to N it permits N holders, which makes it the natural expression of a resource pool. A mutex is the case N=1.

cards.q: Why must a condition variable always be waited on in a while loop?
cards.a: Because of spurious wakeups, and because another thread may have consumed the condition before you were scheduled.

cards.q: Name Coffman's four conditions for deadlock and say which one you break.
cards.a: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. In practice you break circular wait, with lock ordering: define a total order over all locks and always acquire in it — which is why multi-row database code should sort identifiers first.

cards.q: Distinguish deadlock, livelock, starvation and the thundering herd.
cards.a: Deadlock: nothing runs. Livelock: threads run and respond to each other but nothing completes. Starvation: a thread never gets the resource because others keep taking it. Thundering herd: releasing wakes every waiter, all of whom race and all but one sleep again — hence waking one.

cards.q: Why is Redis single-threaded, and what is the price?
cards.a: Every command is atomic by construction — no locks, races, deadlock or coherence traffic — which is why INCR is a correct distributed counter and a Lua script is atomic. The price is that one slow command blocks everything (KEYS * on a large database is an outage, hence SCAN) and that commands use one core. Redis 6 threaded the socket I/O while keeping execution single-threaded.

cards.q: How do you diagnose a lock wait in Postgres?
cards.a: pg_stat_activity: wait_event_type = 'Lock' means waiting on another transaction, 'LWLock' means internal shared memory. pg_blocking_pids() names the blocker. Postgres detects deadlocks after deadlock_timeout (1 s) and aborts one transaction with an error you can catch and retry — unusually generous; most systems just hang.

cards.q: Why is a distributed lock not a lock?
cards.a: Nothing guarantees the holder has not vanished. A GC pause, CPU throttling or a partition can exceed the lease, after which two processes believe they hold it. The fix is a fencing token — a monotonically increasing number passed with every write and rejected by the storage layer if lower than the highest seen. Without fencing it reduces contention rather than guaranteeing correctness.

cards.q: Why does async-mutex work without atomics, and where does it fail?
cards.a: It is a promise chain, and JavaScript's run-to-completion means the acquire check and set cannot be interleaved. It is correct within one Node process and gives you exactly nothing across cluster workers or replicas.

cards.q: What actually happens when a process blocks on read?
cards.a: The syscall enters the kernel; the socket buffer is empty; the task's state becomes S; it is added to that socket's wait queue; the scheduler picks something else. Later a packet arrives, the kernel walks the wait queue and marks the task runnable, and it eventually copies the bytes and returns.

cards.q: Correct the claim that blocking wastes CPU.
cards.a: A blocked process consumes exactly zero processor time. The cost is not cycles — it is that this thread can do nothing else, so many clients need many threads, and threads are the expensive thing.

cards.q: Name the three pre-event-loop server architectures and what each traded.
cards.a: Process per connection (inetd, Apache prefork): robust, a crash contained, and expensive. Thread per connection (Apache worker, classic servlet containers): cheaper, still a stack and a scheduler entry each. Bounded thread pool: bounds resource use and introduces head-of-line blocking.

cards.q: Run the C10K arithmetic for thread-per-connection.
cards.a: ~100 KB per thread all-in is 1 GB of memory before any application data; ten thousand tasks in the scheduler; and at ten events per second per connection, 100,000 wake-ups per second at a few microseconds each — a large fraction of a core spent purely switching. Worst of all, the caches never hold anything useful.

cards.q: State the event loop's advantage and its exact boundary.
cards.a: One thread learns about many ready connections in one call and handles each with a function call: nanoseconds and warm caches, and a few hundred bytes per connection instead of ~100 KB. It says nothing about computation — if each event needs 10 ms of processing, one thread handles a hundred per second.

cards.q: Why was nginx written, and what did it beat Apache at?
cards.a: Igor Sysoev, released October 2004, specifically against C10K: an event-driven architecture with one worker process per core. Under many idle or slow connections — which is what the real internet is — it used a fraction of the memory and stayed responsive where Apache thrashed.

cards.q: What was Ryan Dahl's stated argument for Node.js in 2009?
cards.a: That Apache's concurrency model was wrong, and that existing languages made non-blocking code painful because they had blocking standard libraries and no natural callback idiom. JavaScript had no I/O library to deprecate and already had closures.

cards.q: What makes Node's non-blocking guarantee actually hold?
cards.a: That there is no alternative — a library cannot accidentally block the loop with a blocking read because the blocking read is not exposed. Except the Sync functions, which is why using them outside startup is the cardinal error.

cards.q: Why is a database connection pool a bounded thread pool?
cards.a: It has all the same properties: 20 connections serving 200 concurrent requests means 180 waiting, invisibly, inside your process; and one slow query holds a connection while everything behind it waits — head-of-line blocking. Instrument acquisition wait time and queue depth, use statement timeouts, and separate pools for fast and slow work.

cards.q: Why does Slowloris defeat thread-per-connection and not an event loop?
cards.a: Each slowly-held connection occupies a thread in the first design, so a few hundred exhaust the pool with almost no bandwidth. In an event loop each costs a socket and a few hundred bytes. Header and body timeouts still exist because the resource is small but not zero.

cards.q: Why is a 200 ms JSON.parse categorically different in Node than in a threaded server?
cards.a: In thread-per-connection it delays one client. In an event loop it delays every client, because there is one thread and it is not preemptible. Measuring it is what monitorEventLoopDelay is for — the single most valuable metric a Node service can export.

cards.q: Why is a loop over ten thousand non-blocking descriptors not a solution?
cards.a: It makes ten thousand system calls per pass and almost all return EAGAIN. At 50–100 ns each, one pass costs a millisecond of pure overhead and typically finds nothing.

cards.q: Name select's three structural problems.
cards.a: FD_SETSIZE is 1024, compiled into the bitmap type; you rebuild and re-pass the entire set every call because the call destroys it, and the kernel copies and scans all of it; and the return tells you how many are ready, not which, so you scan all n again.

cards.q: State the wrong scaling property in one sentence.
cards.a: The cost is proportional to the number of connections you have rather than the number of events that happened — which is exactly wrong for servers holding many mostly-idle connections.

cards.q: What did poll fix and what did it leave?
cards.a: It replaced the fixed-size bitmap with an array that is not destroyed, so there is no 1024 limit and no rebuilding. The array is still passed in full, copied, and scanned every call. An ergonomic improvement, not an architectural one.

cards.q: How does epoll achieve O(1), mechanically?
cards.a: Registering a descriptor attaches a callback to that socket's wait queue. When the network softirq appends data, that callback pushes the descriptor onto the epoll instance's ready list. So the list is maintained continuously by the events themselves, and epoll_wait does not scan — it hands back the list.

cards.q: Distinguish level-triggered from edge-triggered, and say who uses which.
cards.a: Level-triggered reports readiness as long as data remains, so a partial read is safe. Edge-triggered reports only the transition, so failing to drain to EAGAIN means the connection hangs silently — faster, and unforgiving. libuv is level-triggered; nginx is edge-triggered.

cards.q: Name the four platform mechanisms libuv hides.
cards.a: epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD/macOS, Jonathan Lemon, FreeBSD 4.1, 2000 — arguably a better design, handling timers, signals and file events through one interface), IOCP (Windows, completion-based rather than readiness-based), and Solaris event ports.

cards.q: Why can a regular file not be polled for readiness?
cards.a: Readiness answers 'will this block?', and for a file the answer is always that you can read it — the real question is how long, which readiness cannot express. epoll returns EPERM for regular files, and O_NONBLOCK is simply ignored on them.

cards.q: Given that, what are the only three possible responses, and which did Node take?
cards.a: Use threads (libuv's threadpool — Node's answer, and the reason UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE exists); use POSIX aio, widely regarded as broken; or use io_uring, a completion-based interface that works properly, which libuv adopted for some file operations from 1.45 (2023).

cards.q: What does strace on an idle Node server show, and what does that tell you?
cards.a: One line: a blocked epoll_wait. That is the entire runtime at rest, consuming zero CPU. Under load it becomes epoll_wait returning, a burst of read/write/futex, and back.

cards.q: Why can a slow DNS server stall your file reads?
cards.a: dns.lookup calls getaddrinfo, a blocking library function, so it runs on the shared libuv threadpool alongside file I/O, crypto and zlib. Four threads by default. Use dns.resolve, which speaks DNS over a socket and goes through epoll.

cards.q: What is EMFILE, why is 1024 the classic limit, and how do you diagnose it?
cards.a: The per-process descriptor table is full. 1024 is a fossil of select's FD_SETSIZE. Diagnose with ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l and lsof -p; usually it is a leak — unconsumed HTTP responses, unclosed streams, connections without keep-alive timeouts — and a leak exhausts any limit.

cards.q: What is backpressure at the socket level, and what happens if you ignore it?
cards.a: A full send buffer makes a non-blocking write return short, and the correct response is to register for EPOLLOUT. Node surfaces this as write() returning false and a later 'drain'. Ignoring it means Node buffers the unwritten data in your heap without limit — which is how streaming a large file to a slow client exhausts memory. pipeline() handles it, which is the real reason to prefer it.

cards.q: What kind of thing is the event loop, precisely?
cards.a: A scheduler in user space. Everything from Node 7 applies, with one decisive difference: it has no timer interrupt and no privileged mode, so it is cooperative and regains control only when a callback returns.

cards.q: Name libuv's phases in order.
cards.a: timers; pending callbacks (deferred system operations, chiefly certain TCP errors); idle and prepare (internal); poll (the only phase that blocks); check (setImmediate); close callbacks.

cards.q: How is the poll timeout computed, in three cases?
cards.a: Zero if setImmediate callbacks are pending, since the check phase has work. The time until the nearest timer if any — which is how setTimeout is implemented, with no timer syscall and no timer thread. Otherwise infinite, which is why an idle Node process uses zero CPU.

cards.q: Why does a Node process exit, and why does a forgotten setInterval prevent it?
cards.a: There is no 'main is finished' concept — the loop exits when nothing at all is pending: no handles, no requests, no timers. A live timer or an unclosed server is pending work.

cards.q: Where do process.nextTick and microtasks run?
cards.a: Not in any phase — after every single callback and between every phase transition, drained completely including anything added while draining. nextTick first, entirely, then microtasks, entirely.

cards.q: How can process.nextTick hang a process?
cards.a: A nextTick that schedules another loops forever without the loop advancing: no I/O served, no timers, apparently hung at 100% CPU. The same is true of a recursively resolving promise chain. setImmediate cannot do this because it lands in the next iteration's check phase.

cards.q: Where does the code after an await run relative to timers and I/O?
cards.a: Before both. The continuation is queued as a microtask, so await is a very cheap yield rather than a trip through the loop. await on a non-promise still yields and still costs a microtask turn.

cards.q: Why is setTimeout(f,0) vs setImmediate(g) nondeterministic at the top level but deterministic inside an I/O callback?
cards.a: At the top level the 1 ms clamp may or may not have elapsed by the time the loop first reaches timers, depending on startup duration. Inside an I/O callback the loop is in the poll phase and check comes immediately after, while timers are a full iteration away — so setImmediate always wins.

cards.q: Describe one iteration of the browser's event loop.
cards.a: Take one task from a task queue and run it to completion; perform a microtask checkpoint, draining that queue entirely; then, if it is time to render, run the rendering steps.

cards.q: Name the browser's rendering steps in order.
cards.a: requestAnimationFrame callbacks; recalculate style; layout; update the compositing tree; paint. Then requestIdleCallback if time remains before the next frame.

cards.q: Why is requestAnimationFrame the correct place for visual changes and setTimeout(f,16) not?
cards.a: rAF runs immediately before style and layout, so changes are applied in the same frame with no intermediate paint. A timer lands in a task queue with no relationship to the frame boundary, producing jitter and dropped frames.

cards.q: What is layout thrashing and why does batching fix it?
cards.a: Reading a geometric property (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop) forces the browser to flush pending style and layout to answer correctly. Alternating writes and reads forces a layout per iteration; all reads then all writes makes it one.

cards.q: Why does React's scheduler use MessageChannel rather than setTimeout?
cards.a: To avoid the 4 ms clamp on nested timeouts. It yields roughly every 5 ms so the browser can take input and paint — a cooperative scheduler inside a cooperative scheduler inside a preemptive one.

cards.q: What are event loop delay and event loop utilisation, and why export both?
cards.a: Delay is the time between when a callback was due and when it ran — it tells you whether the loop is being blocked and by how much. Utilisation is the fraction of time the loop spent working rather than waiting in epoll_wait — it tells you how close to saturated the process is, and is a better autoscaling signal than CPU. A p99 delay of 200 ms at 40% CPU is a complete diagnosis.

cards.q: List everything that blocks the event loop.
cards.a: Any *Sync call; JSON.parse/stringify on a large object; synchronous crypto or compression; a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS); a large synchronous loop; a deep structuredClone; template rendering of a large page; and a very large number of pending microtasks, since they drain fully before the loop advances.

cards.q: Match the fixes to the causes.
cards.a: Chunk with setImmediate to yield between chunks; move CPU-bound work to a worker thread; move heavy or slow work to a separate process or a queue; stream instead of buffering; or push it into the database if it is really a data operation. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE does nothing for main-thread blocking.
